hints: A Type I error is made when the null hypothesis $p = 0.9$ is rejected although it is actually true. Say what 'reject $\text{H}_0$' means for Marie's conclusion about Jacques' customers.
walkthrough:
**What a Type I error is**

In any hypothesis test there are two ways to go wrong. A **Type I error** means we **reject the null hypothesis $\text{H}_0$ when $\text{H}_0$ is actually true**.

(The other way, a Type II error, is accepting $\text{H}_0$ when it is false. It is not asked here.)

**Put it in the context of Jacques**

Here $\text{H}_0$ is $p = 0.9$: Jacques is right and 90% of his customers are satisfied.

Rejecting $\text{H}_0$ means Marie concludes that fewer than 90% of customers are satisfied. So a Type I error is: Marie concludes that the percentage of satisfied customers is less than 90%, **when in fact it is 90%**.

The question says 'in the context', so you must mention the customers or their satisfaction. Writing only 'rejecting $\text{H}_0$ when it is true' does not earn the mark.

**Final answer**

A Type I error is Marie concluding that less than 90% of Jacques' customers are satisfied, when the true percentage is 90%.

hints: A Type I error happens when $\text{H}_0$ is true, so $p = 0.9$ and the number satisfied is $X \sim \text{B}(15,\ 0.9)$. Marie rejects when fewer than 12 are satisfied, so you need $\text{P}(X \leqslant 11)$. This is quicker as $1 - \text{P}(X \geqslant 12)$.
Write out the terms for $X = 15, 14, 13, 12$ with the binomial formula $\binom{15}{r}\,0.9^r\,(1 - 0.9)^{15-r}$. Start with $0.9^{15} + 15 \times 0.9^{14} \times (1 - 0.9)$.
Add the terms for $X = 13$ and $X = 12$ in the same way ($\binom{15}{2}$ and $\binom{15}{3}$ come from choosing the unsatisfied customers), then subtract the whole sum from 1. Give 3 s.f.
walkthrough:
**What we are finding**

The probability of a Type I error is the probability of rejecting $\text{H}_0$ **when $\text{H}_0$ is true**. So we pretend $p = 0.9$ is true and find the chance that Marie's rule rejects it.

Marie rejects $\text{H}_0$ if fewer than 12 customers are satisfied. So we need $\text{P}(X < 12) = \text{P}(X \leqslant 11)$.

**Why binomial**

There are a fixed number of customers (15), each is either satisfied or not, they are independent, and each has the same chance 0.9 of being satisfied (if $\text{H}_0$ is true). So $X$, the number satisfied, follows a binomial distribution:

$$X \sim \text{B}(15,\ 0.9)$$

**Use the complement to save work**

$\text{P}(X \leqslant 11)$ would need twelve terms ($X = 0$ up to $11$). The opposite event $X \geqslant 12$ needs only four terms ($X = 12, 13, 14, 15$). So:

$$\text{P}(X \leqslant 11) = 1 - \text{P}(X \geqslant 12) = 1 - \big(\text{P}(X = 15) + \text{P}(X = 14) + \text{P}(X = 13) + \text{P}(X = 12)\big)$$

The first M1 is for an attempt at this, with up to one end error allowed.

**The binomial formula**

For $X \sim \text{B}(n, p)$: $\text{P}(X = r) = \binom{n}{r} p^r (1-p)^{n-r}$. Here $n = 15$, $p = 0.9$, and $1 - p = 0.1$.

**The first two terms (first M1)**

$X = 15$: all 15 satisfied. $\binom{15}{15} = 1$, so $\text{P}(X = 15) = 0.9^{15} = 0.205891$.

$X = 14$: one customer is not satisfied. $\binom{15}{14} = 15$.

$$\text{P}(X = 14) = 15 \times 0.9^{14} \times 0.1 = 15 \times 0.228768 \times 0.1 = 0.343152$$

**The next two terms (second M1)**

$X = 13$: two not satisfied. $\binom{15}{2} = \dfrac{15 \times 14}{2} = 105$.

$$\text{P}(X = 13) = 105 \times 0.9^{13} \times 0.1^2 = 105 \times 0.254187 \times 0.01 = 0.266896$$

$X = 12$: three not satisfied. $\binom{15}{3} = \dfrac{15 \times 14 \times 13}{3 \times 2 \times 1} = 455$.

$$\text{P}(X = 12) = 455 \times 0.9^{12} \times 0.1^3 = 455 \times 0.282430 \times 0.001 = 0.128505$$

Quick check: you can also get all four with your calculator's binomial pdf (n = 15, p = 0.9) for $x = 12, 13, 14, 15$.

**Add up and take from 1**

$$0.205891 + 0.343152 + 0.266896 + 0.128505 = 0.944444$$

$$\text{P}(X \leqslant 11) = 1 - 0.944444 = 0.055556$$

This earns the A1. Keep at least 5 decimal places in the sum; rounding the four terms too early can give $0.0555$, which the scheme also accepts.

**Final answer**

The probability of a Type I error is $0.0556$ (3 s.f.). The scheme also accepts $0.0555$.
